Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Kiet is a 40-year-old divorced journalist of Vietnamese heritage who was kidnapped and tortured while investigating forced labour camps in a neighbouring country. For three weeks he was blindfolded, beaten, starved, and forced to listen as other prisoners—children among them—cried in adjacent cells. He was eventually released in a prisoner exchange, but the physical and psychological scars remained deeply embedded.

In the months that followed, Kiet found himself unable to return to his previous life. He began to notice that the sound of a child crying—any child, anywhere—would send a jolt of electricity through his chest, and in those moments his memory of the cell would feel vivid yet impossible, as though the whole ordeal had happened to someone else. Hearing a name that resembled one of his captors would trigger a visceral sense of dizziness, leaving him lightheaded and convinced that others could see the shame written on his face. That feeling that people could read his history just by looking at him made him certain he was fundamentally broken, and he started avoiding colleagues he had socialised with before the kidnapping, certain they pitied or judged him.

What frightened Kiet most was how ordinary sounds now made him jump. A car door slamming, a spoon clattering against a bowl—each unexpected noise reignited the hypervigilance he had relied on in captivity. Once that hypervigilance took hold, almost any sensation could become a trigger — a car door, a child’s laugh, the rhythm of footsteps behind him — because his body was already braced for danger. When he found himself scanning faces in a coffee shop for signs of threat, he would be flooded with guilt and anger, believing that his cooperation under torture—giving up a source’s name—had violated his core ethics. This belief that he was cowardly and untrustworthy meant that even a stranger’s neutral glance or a brief silence in conversation now felt like exposure, as if his shame must be visible on his skin. He dwelled endlessly on how he could have prevented his capture, replaying decisions with a tight, obsessive focus, which only amplified his startle response and made him more vigilant. He also stopped eating properly, restricting food as a way to regain control; but the resulting light-headedness often made him feel dizzy again, and that dizziness would pull him back into the unreal fragments of his memory.

Kiet’s memory of the torture itself was riddled with gaps. Deliberate effort to recall only brought up disjointed sensations—pressure on his wrists, the taste of blood—but never a coherent story. The gaps themselves felt threatening, as if something hidden might ambush him, and they reinforced his belief that he was defective, that his mind had broken. Because the gaps left him no coherent story to hold onto, he found himself scanning ordinary sounds and scenes for clues that might fill the void, so that a door closing or a certain angle of light now struck him as a possible warning. In turn, his hypervigilance made deliberate recall even harder, because he was always scanning, never able to sit still with the past. When he did catch a glimpse of a memory, it felt so extreme that he found it hard to accept it had really happened; that sense of unreality only deepened his conviction that others saw him as damaged.

As weeks turned into months, Kiet’s avoidance narrowed his world. He stopped going to the newsroom, worked from home, and saw almost no one. But the streets and sounds he avoided had become saturated with meaning: the route he no longer took to the café, the ringtone he silenced, the colleague he crossed the street to avoid — each absence was itself a reminder, and the avoidance turned the city into a net of triggers. His ex-wife had stopped calling after he cancelled their son’s visit three times—the boy’s crying had become unbearable. The loneliness fed his rumination, and rumination brought him back to the memory gaps, which in turn drove him to restrict food even more. He came to believe that the more he ate, the more he would feel his body and the more his past would surface. The cycle was tightening, and he could feel his career slipping away.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a breakdown during a routine assignment: a colleague mentioned a name similar to his torturer’s, and Kiet became so dizzy and nauseated that he had to be taken to the emergency room. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, but also quietly desperate to believe that the person he was before—a reporter who trusted his own instincts—still exists somewhere beneath the shame and the startle.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs of being broken or judged) cause or heighten sensitivity to triggers.
No paragraph conveys that memory (gaps, fragments) leads to the experience or detection of triggers.
No paragraph conveys that threat (hypervigilance, startle) directly causes the occurrence or salience of triggers.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, food restriction) lead to the emergence or perception of triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs of being broken or judged) cause or heighten sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that memory (gaps, fragments) leads to the experience or detection of triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that threat (hypervigilance, startle) directly causes the occurrence or salience of triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, food restriction) lead to the emergence or perception of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
